title: Error-Generator-Level Compression for Fast Quantum Gates
abstract: Fast quantum gates in multilevel systems require suppressing many coherent-error channels using pulses that remain simple to implement. We introduce error-generator-level compression, a Magnus-based control principle that minimizes the complete projected error generator at a chosen perturbative order while restricting the implemented waveform to a few independently adjustable coefficients. This construction preserves all modeled computational and leakage errors rather than truncating the pulse by error channel, while its generator-level objective directly penalizes residual eigenphases that can signal departure from the perturbative regime. For fast transmon gates, a three-parameter pulse suppresses errors by orders of magnitude, outperforms grid-optimized leading- order DRAG over the gate-time range studied, and approaches a fully parameterized 17-parameter Magnus correction. The compressed pulse is also substantially less sensitive to the illustrative finite-bandwidth filtering model considered here.
summary: The paper presents Error-Generator-Level Compression, a novel Magnus-based control method designed to suppress complex coherent errors in fast quantum gates using minimal control parameters. By minimizing a penalty functional derived from the projected error generator, it achieves superior gate fidelity compared to existing techniques like DRAG. This approach is particularly valuable for superconducting qubits as it maintains physical insight into error sources while simplifying pulse design.
main_problem: The core problem is suppressing high-dimensional coherent error channels during fast quantum gate operations while ensuring the required control pulse remains simple to implement.
main_result: A novel 'Error-Generator-Level Compression' technique using a Magnus-based principle successfully suppresses errors by orders of magnitude, achieving target fidelity faster than established methods like DRAG.
method: The authors introduce error-generator-level compression, which minimizes the projected error generator at a perturbative order while constraining the control waveform to only a few adjustable coefficients.
model_or_system: The study focuses on fast quantum gates implemented on transmon qubits, modeled by a driven Hamiltonian that includes terms for target evolution and coherent errors. The analysis uses a four-level truncation of the system dynamics.
key_observables: Average fidelity error ($\epsilon$), projected error generator ($\hat{E}_{	ext{rel}}$), and residual eigenphases (diagnostics).
important_parameters: The number of adjustable pulse parameters (e.g., three for the compressed pulse vs. 17 for full correction) and the gate time scale ($|\alpha_2| t_f$).
main_assumptions: The method does not make the truncated Magnus expansion exact; it selects a low-dimensional pulse by penalizing nonperturbatively large residual eigenphases.
figures_summary: Figures compare error suppression and fidelity performance across different control methods (compressed vs. DRAG) and demonstrate that the compressed pulse is less sensitive to finite-bandwidth filtering than fully parameterized pulses.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of high-dimensional error suppression, details the Magnus-based compression principle by minimizing a spectral penalty on the projected error generator, rigorously relates this functional minimization to the average fidelity error, and finally tests the robustness against realistic finite-bandwidth filtering effects.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, physically motivated control technique that directly targets the structure of coherent errors in superconducting qubits, offering an alternative to standard unitary optimization methods by focusing on the underlying error generators.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Schematic comparison between fidelity-based com- pression and generator-level compression. Minimizing a final- time unitary objective can favor nonperturbative solutions because the unitary is periodic in the residual eigenphases. In contrast, compressed Magnus control evaluates a spectral penalty that is convex in the Hermitian diagnostic genera- tor and is minimized when the projected residual eigenphases vanish; the induced landscape in pulse coeﬀicients need not be convex.
